newsitem.title: UK: UK ethnic minorities get raw deal on cancer care.
newsitem.headline: UK ethnic minorities get raw deal on cancer care.

text.p: Britain's ethnic minorities are second-class citizens when it comes to getting cancer care, according to a report published on Thursday.
The Cancer Research Campaign said there was a lower uptake of breast and cervical screening among minority ethnic groups in Britain than among the rest of the population.
"We are extremely worried that lives could be at risk because people from ethnic minorities in Britain are second class citizens when it comes to cancer services," said spokeswoman Jean King.
"This is because cancer services are not always culturally sensitive enough, and because there is not enough awareness about cancer among the ethnic minority communities themselves," she added.
King said it was impossible to assess the size of the problem because of the lack of widespread data available on cancer incidence and mortality among ethnic minority groups in Britain.

The charity said it feared Britain may be mirroring the United States where studies have shown that white cancer patients had up to 20 percent better chance of survival than black patients five years after diagnosis for certain cancers.

Researchers in the northern English city of Bradford found that women from ethnic minority groups often did not attend screening sessions for breast and cervical cancer because they were concerned they might be seen by a male doctor.
Other women failed to turn up for appointments because their names had been misspelt or because they were not aware of the implications of screening and cancer.
The Cancer Research Campaign said it had teamed up with health department officials to try to tackle the problem.
